items.text: We introduce a new language representation model called BERT, which stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers.
items.why: Introduces the BERT model.
items.plain: We introduce a new language representation model named BERT, which stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers.

items.text: Unlike recent language representation models (Peters et al., 2018a; Radford et al., 2018), BERT is designed to pretrain deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context in all layers.
items.why: Explains core technical distinction of BERT.
items.plain: Unlike recent language models, BERT is designed to pre-train deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by looking at both left and right context in all layers at once.

items.text: As a result, the pre-trained BERT model can be ﬁnetuned with just one additional output layer to create state-of-the-art models for a wide range of tasks, such as question answering and language inference, without substantial taskspeciﬁc architecture modiﬁcations.
items.why: States how BERT is applied to tasks.
items.plain: Because of this pre-training, the model can be fine-tuned with just one extra output layer to build top-performing models for many tasks, such as question answering, without major custom architecture changes.

items.text: It obtains new state-of-the-art results on eleven natural language processing tasks, including pushing the GLUE score to 80.5% (7.7% point absolute improvement), MultiNLI accuracy to 86.7% (4.6% absolute improvement), SQuAD v1.1 question answering Test F1 to 93.2 (1.5 point absolute improvement) and SQuAD v2.0 Test F1 to 83.1 (5.1 point absolute improvement).
items.why: Summarizes the paper's main empirical benchmark results.
items.plain: It sets new state-of-the-art results on eleven natural language processing tasks, including raising the GLUE score to 80.5% (a 7.7% absolute improvement), MultiNLI accuracy to 86.7% (a 4.6% improvement), SQuAD v1.1 question answering Test F1 to 93.2 (a 1.5 point improvement), and SQuAD v2.0 Test F1 to 83.1 (a 5.1 point improvement).

items.text: The major limitation is that standard language models are unidirectional, and this limits the choice of architectures that can be used during pre-training.
items.why: Identifies the core problem with previous models.
items.plain: The main limitation of standard language models is that they only look in one direction, which restricts the architectures that can be used during pre-training.

items.text: BERT alleviates the previously mentioned unidirectionality constraint by using a “masked language model” (MLM) pre-training objective, inspired by the Cloze task (Taylor, 1953).
items.why: Explains how BERT solves unidirectionality.
items.plain: BERT overcomes the single-direction limitation by using a masked language model training objective.

items.text: Unlike left-toright language model pre-training, the MLM objective enables the representation to fuse the left and the right context, which allows us to pretrain a deep bidirectional Transformer.
items.why: Explains benefit of the masked language model.
items.plain: The masked language model objective allows the model to combine left and right context, enabling pre-training of a deep bidirectional Transformer.

items.text: In addition to the masked language model, we also use a “next sentence prediction” task that jointly pretrains text-pair representations.
items.why: Mentions the second pre-training task.
items.plain: In addition to the masked language model, we use a next sentence prediction task to pre-train representations of sentence pairs.

items.text: BERT is the ﬁrst ﬁnetuning based representation model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on a large suite of sentence-level and token-level tasks, outperforming many task-speciﬁc architectures.
items.why: Summarizes key claim regarding fine-tuning models.
items.plain: BERT is the first fine-tuning-based representation model to achieve state-of-the-art performance across a large suite of sentence-level and token-level tasks, outperforming customized architectures.

items.text: A distinctive feature of BERT is its uniﬁed architecture across different tasks.
items.why: Highlights unified architecture feature.
items.plain: A key feature of BERT is that it uses a unified architecture across different tasks.

items.text: Both BERTBASE and BERTLARGE outperform all systems on all tasks by a substantial margin, obtaining 4.5% and 7.0% respective average accuracy improvement over the prior state of the art.
items.why: Highlights GLUE benchmark results.
items.plain: Both BERT-BASE and BERT-LARGE outperform all previous systems across all GLUE tasks by a substantial margin, improving average accuracy by 4.5% and 7.0% respectively over the prior state of the art.

items.text: Our best performing system outperforms the top leaderboard system by +1.5 F1 in ensembling and +1.3 F1 as a single system.
items.why: States SQuAD v1.1 performance result.
items.plain: Our best performing system outperforms the top leaderboard system on SQuAD v1.1 by +1.5 F1 in ensembling and +1.3 F1 as a single system.

items.text: We observe a +5.1 F1 improvement over the previous best system.
items.why: States SQuAD v2.0 performance result.
items.plain: We observe a +5.1 F1 improvement over the previous best system on SQuAD 2.0.

items.text: BERTLARGE outperforms the authors’ baseline ESIM+ELMo system by +27.1% and OpenAI GPT by 8.3%.
items.why: States SWAG benchmark result.
items.plain: BERT-LARGE outperforms the authors' baseline system by +27.1% and OpenAI GPT by 8.3% on the SWAG dataset.

items.text: However, we believe that this is the ﬁrst work to demonstrate convincingly that scaling to extreme model sizes also leads to large improvements on very small scale tasks, provided that the model has been sufﬁciently pre-trained.
items.why: States key takeaway on scaling model size.
items.plain: We show that scaling to extreme model sizes leads to large performance improvements even on very small-scale tasks, provided the model has been sufficiently pre-trained.

items.text: This demonstrates that BERT is effective for both ﬁnetuning and feature-based approaches.
items.why: States conclusion on applicability.
items.plain: This demonstrates that BERT works effectively for both fine-tuning and feature-based approaches.

items.text: Our major contribution is further generalizing these ﬁndings to deep bidirectional architectures, allowing the same pre-trained model to successfully tackle a broad set of NLP tasks.
items.why: Summarizes the main contribution of the paper.
items.plain: Our main contribution is generalizing language model pre-training to deep bidirectional architectures, allowing a single pre-trained model to handle a broad range of NLP tasks.

items.text: Among the three, only BERT representations are jointly conditioned on both left and right context in all layers.
items.why: Highlights BERT's core architectural distinction of joint bidirectionality across all layers.
items.plain: Out of the three models, only BERT represents text by jointly considering both left and right context across all layers.

items.text: The core argument of this work is that the bi-directionality and the two pretraining tasks presented in Section 3.1 account for the majority of the empirical improvements, but we do note that there are several other differences between how BERT and GPT were trained:
items.why: States the central claim regarding bidirectionality and pretraining tasks driving performance gains.
items.plain: The main argument of this work is that bidirectional context and the two pre-training tasks cause most of the performance improvements.

items.text: To isolate the effect of these differences, we perform ablation experiments in Section 5.1 which demonstrate that the majority of the improvements are in fact coming from the two pre-training tasks and the bidirectionality they enable.
items.why: Summarizes ablation results confirming the main source of BERT's performance improvements.
items.plain: Ablation experiments show that most of the improvements come from the two pre-training tasks and the bidirectional processing they allow.

items.text: Answer: Yes, BERTBASE achieves almost 1.0% additional accuracy on MNLI when trained on 1M steps compared to 500k steps.
items.why: Provides a specific metric confirming the benefit of long pretraining duration.
items.plain: Training the base model for 1,000,000 steps instead of 500,000 steps increases its accuracy on the MNLI task by almost 1.0%.

items.text: However, in terms of absolute accuracy the MLM model begins to outperform the LTR model almost immediately.
items.why: States that masked pretraining outperforms traditional left-to-right pretraining in absolute accuracy.
items.plain: In terms of overall accuracy, the masked language model outperforms the left-to-right model almost immediately.
